title: Joseph Calasanz (25 August)
hook: he opened the first free public school in Europe (1597)
tomorrow: The death of John the Baptist (29 August)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartholomew, the honest doubter who heard come and see. Your line was without guile. Where did honesty cost you something yesterday? Day one thousand nineteen.

Joseph Calasanz came to Rome, the story goes, hoping for a good church post. A priest from Spain with plans. Then he started noticing the children. In the poor streets of the city they were everywhere: running loose, working, getting into trouble. None of them in school, because school cost money and their families had none. He asked the parish to teach them. No room. He asked others. Nobody took it on. So he did it himself. He found rooms, gathered the children, and taught them reading, writing, sums and the faith, and charged nothing. The good church post never mattered again. Today, the priest who opened schools that didn't charge.
screen: `A PRIEST WITH PLANS.` → `CHILDREN WITH NO SCHOOL.` → `SO HE DID IT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: He called them the Pious Schools, and the order he founded to run them is known as the Piarists. The idea was simple and, for its time, bold: a poor child's mind is worth teaching, properly, and for free. Not charity on the side. Real lessons, every day, alongside prayer. Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "he that shall receive one such little child in my name, receiveth me." Calasanz took that literally. Every child who came through the door was a guest of that kind. The schools grew. Other teachers joined. And then, near the end of his life, the story turns hard. Men inside his own order worked against him. He was removed from leading it, and the order itself was cut down and stripped of its standing. Everything he had built looked finished. Here is what tradition remembers: he didn't fight it with bitterness. He kept praying, kept obeying, kept teaching where he could, and forgave the men who had done it. He died with the work in ruins. And after his death, the order was restored, and the schools went on. The Church later named him a patron of Christian schools. So the lesson has two halves. The first is about who deserves an education: everyone, including the child whose family can't pay. The second is about what you do when the good thing you built is taken from you. Calasanz's answer, in the story, was patience, and it outlived the men who opposed him.
screen: `THE PIOUS SCHOOLS.` · `RECEIVE ONE SUCH LITTLE CHILD.` · `TURNED ON BY HIS OWN.` · `RESTORED AFTER HIS DEATH.` · then, large: `FREE SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take stock of what you could teach. Settle, and breathe. Calasanz started with what he had: reading, writing, sums. Ask what you have. A skill your hands know. A language. How to fix a bike, read a bill, cook one good meal. Pick one thing. Then think of who might need it: a child down the street, a neighbor, someone new in town. Don't plan the whole lesson. Just see the two of you, and the thing passing between you. Then think of the children, near or far, who are learning right now with very little. If you pray, you can ask Saint Joseph Calasanz to pray for that child. If you don't, just hold them in mind with hope. The bell holds the time.
Joseph Calasanz. The priest who opened free schools for poor children in Rome, founded the Piarists, and forgave the men who tore his work down.
Your line: free schools. Today, give something to a school that doesn't charge: a few dollars, a box of books, an hour of help, or just a thank-you note to a teacher. Day one thousand nineteen.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memory of Saint Joseph Calasanz on 25 August; Piarist schools and parishes honor him as their founder, and Catholic teachers ask his prayers for their students.

what a scholar hears: the Piarists take their name from the Scholae Piae; the order was cut down near the end of his life and restored after his death.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'first free public school in Europe (1597)' is a superlative and a date; both left out. The script says only that the schools were free for poor children, and that the idea was 'for its time, bold'. Confirm.
Hook: that he came to Rome seeking a church post (a benefice) is given as 'the story goes'. Confirm.
The order's troubles: he was removed as superior and the order reduced (1646) after internal intrigue; restored after his death. Dates left out. Confirm the summary 'cut down to almost nothing'.
'The Church later named him a patron of Christian schools' (Pius XII). Confirm.
Original: Scholae Piae, ecclesiastical pronunciation. Confirm.

Editor: hook no longer calls him 'patron of schools that don't charge' (his title is patron of Christian schools); 'cut down to almost nothing' softened; practice changed from remembering a teacher (too close to day 1009's remember-who-nursed-you) to taking stock of what you could teach; fork moved from the removed-founder dilemma, which repeated day 1021's fork, to the free-school decision.
